claim: Neuronal physiology depends on a neuron's ion channel composition and unique morphology.
source: Neuronal physiology depends on a neuron's ion channel composition and unique morphology.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about neuronal function.

claim: Variable ion channel compositions can produce similar neuronal physiologies across animals.
source: Variable ion channel compositions can produce similar neuronal physiologies across animals.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction to multiple studies showing ion channel variability.

claim: Theoretical studies suggest that morphology is tightly tuned to minimize wiring and conduction delay of synaptic events.
source: Theoretical studies suggest that moraphology is tightly tuned to minimize wiring and conduction delay of synaptic events.
evidence: This claim references theoretical work cited in the introduction regarding wiring optimization principles.

claim: Four neuron types in the stomatogastric ganglion (STG) of the crab Cancer borealis were characterized using high-resolution confocal microscopy and custom computational tools.
source: We utilize high-resolution confocal microscopy and custom computational tools to characterize the morphologies of four neuron types in the stomatogastric ganglion (STG) of the crab Cancer borealis.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study, which is detailed in the methods section.

claim: Macroscopic branching patterns and fine cable properties are variable within and across neuron types in the STG.
source: Macroscopic branching patterns and fine cable properties are variable within and across neuron types.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by quantitative morphological analyses presented in the results.

claim: STG neurons do not adhere to prevailing hypotheses regarding wiring optimization principles.
source: We compare these neuronal structures to synthetic minimal spanning neurite trees constrained by a wiring cost equation and find that STG neurons do not adhere to prevailing hypotheses regarding wiring optimization principles.
evidence: This conclusion is based on comparison of actual STG neurons to synthetic minimal spanning trees, as shown in the results section.

claim: In the STG circuit, neuronal structures appear to be governed by a space-filling mechanism that outweighs the cost of inefficient wiring.
source: In this highly modulated and oscillating circuit, neuronal structures appear to be governed by a space-filling mechanism that outweighs the cost of inefficient wiring.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the subtree analysis and comparison to wiring optimization models.

claim: Neurons and circuits can function despite remarkable variability in their ion channel composition.
source: Numerous studies have shown that neurons and circuits can function despite remarkable variability in their ion channel composition (Prinz et al., 2004; Schulz et al., 2006; Goaillard et al., 2009; Norris et al., 2011; Roffman et al., 2012; Gutierrez et al., 2013; Sakurai et al., 2014; see Marder and Goaillard (2006), Calabrese et al. (2011) and Marder et al. (2015) for reviews).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Neurons can generate robust, highly conserved firing patterns despite some degree of sloppiness in their underlying physiological parameters.
source: These observations suggest that neurons can generate robust, highly conserved firing patterns despite some degree of sloppiness in their underlying physiological parameters.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies on ion channel variability.

claim: It is often assumed that precise neuronal computations and plasticity rules arise from specialized neuronal morphologies.
source: In contrast, it is often assumed that precise neuronal computations and plasticity rules arise from specialized neuronal morphologies (Mainen and Sejnowski, 1996; Stiefel and Sejnowski, 2007; Cuntz et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement references established assumptions in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Experimental and theoretical studies have argued that optimal wiring principles determine neuronal structure during development.
source: Experimental and theoretical studies have argued that optimal wiring principles determine neuronal structure during development (Chklovskii, 2000, 2004; Chen et al., 2006; Wen and Chklovskii, 2008; Cuntz et al., 2007, 2010, 2012; Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Few studies have reconstructed multiple neurons of the same type at high enough resolution to observe or quantify the stereotypy expected to arise during development.
source: Yet, surprisingly, few studies (Goodman, 1976, 1978; Miller and Jacobs, 1984; Wang et al., 2002; Cuntz et al., 2008, 2010) have reconstructed multiple neurons of the same type at high enough resolution to observe or quantify the stereotypy expected to arise during development, given such optimization principles.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature, supported by limited citations.

claim: Relatively little is known regarding the practical applications of growth rules and the degree of morphological precision required to produce reliable neuronal physiology in varying circuit contexts.
source: Thus, relatively little is known regarding the practical applications of such growth rules and the degree of morphological precision required to produce reliable neuronal physiology in varying circuit contexts.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that motivates the current study.

claim: The 26 neurons of the crab STG have large somata (50–150 µm in diameter) situated around a dense neuropil region.
source: The 26 neurons of the crab STG have large somata (50–150 µm in diameter) situated around a dense neuropil region, wherein synaptic connections are made (Maynard, 1971; Maynard and Dando, 1974; King, 1976a, 1976b; Kilman and Marder, 1996).
evidence: This is an established anatomical fact about the STG, supported by citations.

claim: STG neurons have complex, highly branched structures that ramify throughout the neuropil region.
source: STG neurons have complex, highly branched structures that ramify throughout the neuropil region (Baldwin and Graubard, 1995; Wilensky et al., 2003; Bucher et al., 2007; Thuma et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by previous anatomical studies cited.

claim: STG neurons are subject to modulation by numerous peptides and amines released diffusely in the hemolymph and by descending modulatory inputs.
source: and are subject to modulation by numerous peptides and amines released diffusely in the hemolymph and by descending modulatory inputs (Christie et al., 1995a, 1995b, 1997; Goldberg et al., 1988; Marder et al., 1986; see Marder and Bucher (2007) and Nusbaum and Blitz, 2012 for reviews).
evidence: This is an established characteristic of the STG, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The 14 identified STG neuron types are physiologically defined by their muscle innervation patterns, highly conserved voltage waveforms, and participation in one or both of two rhythms: the fast, ongoing pyloric rhythm and the slow, episodic gastric mill rhythm.
source: The 14 identified STG neuron types are physiologically defined by their muscle innervation patterns (Maynard and Dando, 1974), highly conserved voltage waveforms, and participation in one or both of two rhythms: the fast, ongoing pyloric rhythm and the slow, episodic gastric mill rhythm (Harris-Warrick et al., 1992).
evidence: This describes the physiological characteristics of STG neurons, supported by citations.

claim: STG circuit function is mediated predominately by slow oscillations and graded inhibitory transmission.
source: STG circuit function is mediated predominately by slow oscillations (Graubard and Ross, 1985; Ross and Graubard, 1989) and graded inhibitory transmission (Eisen and Marder, 1982; Marder and Eisen, 1984; Maynard and Walton, 1975; Graubard et al., 1980; Manor et al., 1997, 1999).
evidence: This is an established characteristic of STG circuit function, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Phase relationships between STG neurons can be maintained in the absence of spikes.
source: In fact, phase relationships between STG neurons can be maintained in the absence of spikes (Graubard, 1978; Raper, 1979; Graubard et al., 1983; Anderson and Barker, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: STG neurons are electrotonically compact.
source: Recent work demonstrated that, despite their morphological complexity, STG neurons are electrotonically compact (Otopalik et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the same research group.

claim: Slow voltage events arising from graded synaptic transmission undergo minimal electrotonic decrement across the neuronal structure in STG neurons.
source: Thus, the slow voltage events arising from graded synaptic transmission undergo minimal electrotonic decrement across the neuronal structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited finding that STG neurons are electrotonically compact.

claim: Electrotonic structures of STG neurons could feasibly mask animal-to-animal variability in neuronal morphology within identified STG neuron types.
source: Such electrotonic structures could feasibly mask animal-to-animal variability in neuronal morphology within identified STG neuron types.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the electrotonic properties of STG neurons.

claim: Given their compact electrotonic structures, it is plausible that developmental growth of STG neurons may not be constrained by wiring optimization rules, but perhaps other rules that speak to their role in this highly modulated, oscillating circuit.
source: Additionally, given their compact electrotonic structures, it is plausible that developmental growth of STG neurons may not be constrained by wiring optimization rules, but perhaps other rules that speak to their role in this highly modulated, oscillating circuit.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors that motivates the investigation.

claim: Each STG neuron has a primary neurite that branches extensively throughout the neuropil, forming synapses.
source: The neurons of the STG of the crab Cancer borealis each have a primary neurite that branches extensively throughout the neuropil, forming synapses.
evidence: This is a basic anatomical description of STG neurons.

claim: The primary neurite of STG neurons gives rise to one or multiple axons that project to specific stomach muscles or anterior ganglia.
source: This primary neurite also gives rise to one or multiple axons that project to specific stomach muscles or anterior ganglia (Maynard, 1971; Maynard and Dando, 1974; King, 1976a, 1976b; Kilman and Marder, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The stomatogastric nerve (stn) contains dozens of descending neuromodulatory inputs that branch extensively throughout the neuropil and diffusely release a cocktail of peptides and amines.
source: The stomatogastric nerve (stn) contains dozens of descending neuromodulatory inputs that branch extensively throughout the neuropil and diffusely release a cocktail of peptides and amines (Marder and Bucher, 2007; Nusbaum and Blitz, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: GM, LG, PD, and LP neurons are motor neurons that send axons through either the anterior lateral nerve (aln) or dorsal ventricular nerve (dvn).
source: The four neuron types examined here are motor neurons and send axons through either the anterior lateral nerve (aln) or dorsal ventricular nerve (dvn; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: GM neurons typically have 3–5 axons, with one or multiple axons projecting to the alns and dvn.
source: GM neurons (four copies in each STG) typically have 3–5 axons, with one or multiple axons projecting to the alns and dvn (Figure 1Bi).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1Bi.

claim: LG, PD, and LP neurons project single axons down the dvn.
source: In contrast, the lateral gastric (LG, one copy in each STG), pyloric dilator (PD; two copies in each STG), and lateral pyloric (LP, one copy in each STG) neurons project single axons down the dvn (Figure 1Bii–iv).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1Bii-iv.

claim: Each of the 16 neurons examined had a relatively large soma diameter with a pooled mean ± SD = 125.8 ± 47.5 µm across all neurons.
source: Each of the 16 neurons had a relatively large soma diameter (pooled mean ± SD = 125.8 ± 47.5 µm across all neurons).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: Earlier work in lobster STG suggested some stereotypy in soma positions of certain neuron classes.
source: Earlier work in lobster, Homarus americanus and Panulirus interruptus, STG suggested some stereotypy in soma positions of certain neuron classes (Bucher et al., 2007 and Thuma et al., 2009, respectively).
evidence: This references findings from previous studies.

claim: 75% of the 16 neurons described were situated on the posterior side of the neuropil.
source: Of the 16 neurons described here, 75% were situated on the posterior side of the neuropil (schematized as a gray shaded area).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the study.

claim: Soma locations varied within and across cell types.
source: However, soma locations varied within and across cell types (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Many STG neurite trees contain a 'hand-like' structure, defined as a thick segment that 'sends off a number of secondary neurites' and emerges from a comparatively thin primary neurite.
source: Many STG neurite trees contain a 'hand-like' structure, defined as a thick segment that 'sends off a number of secondary neurites' and emerges from a comparatively thin primary neurite (Example indicated in Figure 1D as 'H'; Bucher et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to a previous study and illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: The hand-like structure was observed in every GM and LG neuron, but not in any LP neurons.
source: This hand-like structure was observed in every GM and LG neuron, but not in any LP neurons.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: Half of the PD neurons had something that could be considered hand-like.
source: Of the neurons used in this study, half of the PD neurons had something that could be considered hand-like.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: LP neurons can be distinguished from other neuron types by their lack of hand-like structures.
source: Thus, relative to the other three neuron types, LP neurons can be distinguished by their lack of hand-like structures.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations about hand-like structures.

claim: 'Hair-like' neurites (very thin <1 µm neurites that are more than 50 µm in length) were observed in all neurons.
source: We also observed the presence of 'hair-like' neurites: very thin (<1 µm) neurites that are more than 50 µm in length in all neurons.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: All 16 neurons examined had more than 10 mm of neurite in their neurite trees.
source: All 16 neurons examined had more than 10 mm of neurite in their neurite trees (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Table 1.

claim: There was a high mean total wiring length across all neurons examined (pooled mean ± SD = 37515 ± 27498 µm; N = 16) with quite a bit of variability across neurons (CV = 0.73; N = 16).
source: Despite a high mean total wiring length across all neurons examined (pooled mean ± SD = 37515 ± 27498 µm; N = 16), there was quite a bit of variability across neurons (CV = 0.73; N = 16).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: GM neurons presented significantly greater mean total wiring lengths relative to the other three neuron types (ANOVA; [F(3,12)=8.34, p=0.0029]; Tukey HSD) with a mean ± SD of 74,890 ± 26581 µm.
source: Across neuron types, GM neurons presented significantly greater mean total wiring lengths relative to the other three neuron types (ANOVA; [F(3,12)=8.34, p=0.0029]; Tukey HSD) with a mean ± SD of 74, 890 ± 26581 µm.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: LG, LP, and PD neurons had within-cell-type mean (± SD) total wirings of 30,583 ± 18,346 µm, 24,321 ± 11,777 µm, and 20,266 ± 65,805 µm, respectively – all less than 50% of the mean GM total wiring length.
source: LG, LP, and PD neurons had within-cell-type mean (± SD) total wirings of 30,583 ± 18,346 µm, 24,321 ± 11,777 µm, and 20,266 ± 65,805 µm, respectively – all less than 50% of the mean GM total wiring length (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study shown in Figure 2A.

claim: GM neurons had a greater number of soma-to-tip neurite paths than the other three neuron types (ANOVA; [F(3,12)=7.14, p=0.0052]; Tukey HSD).
source: GM neurons also had a greater number of soma-to-tip neurite paths (Figure 2B, Table 1; ANOVA; [F(3,12)=7.14, p=0.0052]; Tukey HSD).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: Across and within cell types, there are no apparent trends in Sholl analysis characterization of macroscopic branching patterns.
source: Across and within cell types, there are no apparent trends in this characterization of macroscopic branching patterns.
evidence: This is an observation from the Sholl analysis presented in the study.

claim: Some Sholl distributions are multi-modal, suggesting that there is more branching at certain distances from the soma within each neuron.
source: It is interesting to note, however, that some distributions are multi-modal, suggesting that there is more branching at certain distances from the soma, within each neuron.
evidence: This is an observation from the Sholl analysis.

claim: Based on spatial density plots, there appears to be no obvious patterning in neurite arborizations within each neuron type.
source: Based on these graphical representations, there appears to be no obvious patterning in neurite arborizations within each neuron type.
evidence: This is an observation from the spatial density analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: GM neurons appear to have distinct regions of high neurite density, while PD neurons are more uniformly distributed about the neuropil.
source: Although GM neurons appear to have distinct regions of high neurite density, PD neurons are more uniformly distributed about the neuropil.
evidence: This is an observation from the spatial density analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: GM neurons had greater branch point numbers than the other three cell types (ANOVA, [F(3,12)=7.12, p=0.0053]; Tukey HSD).
source: GM neurons had greater branch point numbers than the other three cell types (ANOVA, [F(3,12)=7.12, p=0.0053]; Tukey HSD; Figure 4A; Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study shown in Figure 4A and Table 1.

claim: Branch angle distributions were similar across cell types and individual neurons.
source: Branch angle distributions were similar across cell types and individual neurons (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an observation from the branch angle analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The majority of branch angles fell between 0 and 100 degrees.
source: The majority of branch angles fell between and 0 and 100 degrees.
evidence: This is an observation from the branch angle analysis.

claim: Mean GM branch angles were 70.7 ± 1.7 (median: 71.4 degrees).
source: Mean GM branch angles were 70.7 ± 1.7 (median: 71.4 degrees).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: LG branch angles averaged 70.6 ± 1.5 (median: 70.7 degrees).
source: Similarly, LG branch angles averaged 70.6 ± 1.5 (median: 70.7 degrees)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: LP branch angles averaged 68.6 ± 0.6 (median: 68.8 degrees).
source: LP branch angles averaged 68.6 ± 0.6 (median: 68.8 degrees)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: PD branch angles had an average value of 70.3 ± 0.8 (median: 70.0 degrees).
source: and PD branch angles had an average value of 70.3 ± 0.8 (median: 70.0 degrees).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: Bifurcations (daughter neurites/branch point = 2) were the most common across all neurons.
source: Bifurcations (daughter neurites/branch point = 2) were the most common across all neurons.
evidence: This is an observation from the branch point type analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Higher order multi-furcations were present in each of the neurons examined.
source: Higher order multi-furcations were also present in each of the neurons examined here.
evidence: This is an observation from the branch point type analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: GM neurons displayed more multi-furcations (with >4 daughter neurites) relative to other neuron types.
source: GM neurons displayed more multi-furcations (with >4 daughter neurites) relative to other neuron types.
evidence: This is an observation from the branch point type analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The differences in the proportions of bi-, tri-, and multi-furcations across cell types are quite small.
source: That said, the differences in the proportions of bi-, tri-, and multi-furcations across cell types are quite small (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an observation from the branch point type analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: For GM, LG, LP, and PD neurons, symmetry index (SI) values (mean ± SD) were 0.48 ± 0.11 (median: 0.51), 0.44 ± 0.11 (median: 0.42), 0.55 ± 0.05 (median: 0.55) and 0.66 ± 0.03 (median: 0.66), respectively.
source: For GM, LG, LP, and PD neurons, SI values (mean ± SD) were 0.48 ± 0.11 (median: 0.51) 0.44 ± 0.11 (median: 0.42), 0.55 ± 0.05 (median: 0.55) and 0.66 ± 0.03 (median: 0.66), respectively (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study shown in Figure 6C.

claim: PD neurons present more symmetrical neurite arborizations relative to other cell types (ANOVA; F(3,12) = 5.45, p=0.01; Tukey HSD).
source: Analysis of mean SI values across cell types (Figure 6D) reveal that PD neurons present more symmetrical neurite arborizations relative to other cell types (ANOVA; F(3,12) = 5.45, p=0.01; Tukey HSD).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Across all neurons, the number of subtrees varied between 2 and 80.
source: Across all neurons, the number of subtrees varied between 2 and 80 (Figure 7A; Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study shown in Figure 7A and Table 1.

claim: GM neurons displayed more subtrees (47 ± 23) than LP (18 ± 6) and PD (6 ± 6) neurons (ANOVA, [F(3,12)=7.6, p=0.0041], Tukey HSD).
source: GM neurons displayed more subtrees (47 ± 23) than LP (18 ± 6) and PD (6 ± 6) neurons. However, there were no other significant distinctions between the other neuron types (Figure 7A; ANOVA, [F(3,12)=7.6, p=0.0041], Tukey HSD).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Subtree numbers are quite variable within each neuron type.
source: As is clear from this scatter plot, subtree numbers are quite variable within each neuron type.
evidence: This is an observation from the subtree analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In 13/16 neurons, the subtree neuritic fields of the actual neurons show less overlap in space than the scrambled-tip populations.
source: In 13/16 neurons, the subtree neuritic fields of the actual neurons show less overlap in space than the scrambled-tip populations.
evidence: This is a finding from the bootstrap analysis of subtree neuritic fields shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Across all neurons, the mean subtree neuritic field radii observed in the actual neuronal subtree arrangements are smaller than those of the scrambled-tip population (bootstrap analyses yielded p-values <0.01 within each neuron).
source: Across all neurons, the mean subtree neuritic field radii observed in the actual neuronal subtree arrangements are smaller than those of the scrambled-tip population (bootstrap analyses yielded p-values <0.01 within each neuron).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the bootstrap analysis shown in Figure 7H.

claim: The actual subtree neuritic fields are more compact relative to those generated by random tip distributions.
source: Thus, the actual subtree neuritic fields are more compact relative to those generated by random tip distributions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the bootstrap analysis.

claim: STG neuronal subtrees may be organized to span the neuropil in a manner that minimizes overlap between subtrees and their neuritic fields.
source: Taken together, this analysis suggests that STG neuronal subtrees may be organized to span the neuropil in a manner that minimizes overlap between subtrees and their neuritic fields.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the subtree analysis results.

claim: The subtree arrangement observed in STG neurons is unlikely to arise from random distribution of terminal tips.
source: This arrangement is unlikely to arise from random distribution of terminal tips.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the bootstrap analysis comparing actual to scrambled tip distributions.

claim: Across all 16 neurons examined, soma-to-tip neurite lengths ranged between 5 and 1778 µm, with the majority of branches ranging between 200 and 800 µm.
source: Across all 16 neurons examined, soma-to-tip neurite lengths ranged between 5 and 1778 µm, with the majority of branches ranging between 200 and 800 µm.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: There are no evident cell-type-specific trends in soma-to-tip neurite length distributions (ANOVA; [F(3,12)=1.48, p=0.2698]; Tukey HSD).
source: There are no evident cell-type-specific trends in soma-to-tip neurite length distributions (ANOVA; [F(3,12)=1.48, p=0.2698]; Tukey HSD).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study shown in Figure 8A.

claim: When all cell types are pooled together, diameter decreases as a function of neurite order (ANOVA [F(3,611)=89.17, p<<0.001]; Tukey HSD).
source: When all cell types are pooled are together, diameter decreases as a function of neurite order (ANOVA [F(3,611)=89.17, p<<0.001]; Tukey HSD; indicated with letters).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The mean 1° diameter across all neurons was 18.7 ± 11.1 µm, and the mean tip diameter across all neurons was 1.5 ± 1.5 µm (mean ± SD).
source: Grouping all neuron types together: 1°, 2°, 3°, and tips have diameters that decreased with each class, such that the mean 1° diameter across all neurons was 18.7 ± 11.1 µm, and the mean tip diameter across all neurons was 1.5 ± 1.5 µm (mean ± SD), respectively (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Diameters varied within each neurite class: 1° neurites presented diameters with a CV = 0.6; 2° diameters varied with CV = 0.9; 3° diameters varied with CV = 1.4; and tip diameters varied with CV = 1.0.
source: However, it should be noted that diameters varied within each neurite class: 1° neurites presented diameters with a CV = 0.6; 2° diameters varied with CV = 0.9; 3° diameters varied with CV = 1.4; and tip diameters varied with CV = 1.0.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of variability from the study.

claim: The calculated Rall powers across individual neurons, cell types, and branch point classes are quite variable and deviate from the optimal 3/2 power.
source: The calculated Rall powers across individual neurons, cell types, and branch point classes are quite variable and deviate from the optimal 3/2 power.
evidence: This is an observation from the Rall power analysis shown in Figure 9 and Table 2.

claim: Mean initial Rall powers were uniformly less than 3/2 across cell types, suggesting that the secondary branches projecting from the primary neurite tend to have large diameters relative to the primary neurite at the branch point junction.
source: Mean initial Rall powers were uniformly less than 3/2, across cell types, suggesting that the secondary branches projecting from the primary neurite tend to have large diameters relative to the primary neurite at the branch point junction.
evidence: This is an observation and interpretation from the Rall power analysis.

claim: P-S, S-T, and terminal branch points presented Rall powers that varied within and across cell types.
source: In contrast, P-S, S-T, and terminal branch points presented Rall powers that varied within and across cell types.
evidence: This is an observation from the Rall power analysis shown in Figure 9 and Table 2.

claim: It does not appear that branch points present optimal parent-daughter radius ratios for current transfer, as predicted by Rall.
source: Taken together, it does not appear that branch points present optimal parent-daughter radius ratios for current transfer, as predicted by Rall.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Rall power analysis.

claim: Across all cell types, tortuosity distributions across all soma-to-tip neurite paths spanned beyond values of 3.
source: Across all cell types, tortuosity distributions across all soma-to-tip neurite paths spanned beyond values of 3 (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is an observation from the tortuosity analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Pooled mean tortuosities within each cell type were uniformly greater than 1, and were: 3.8 (median: 2.6), 4.7 (median: 2.9), 3.2 (median: 2.3), and 2.7 (median: 2.2) for GM, LG, LP, and PD, respectively.
source: Pooled mean tortuosities within each cell type were uniformly greater than 1, and were: 3.8 (median: 2.6), 4.7 (median: 2.9), 3.2 (median: 2.3), and 2.7 (median: 2.2) for GM, LG, LP, and PD, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study shown in Table 1.

claim: By the tortuosity metric, STG neurite paths are measurably longer than the optimal Euclidean length, given their terminal destinations.
source: Thus, by this metric, STG neurite paths are measurably longer than the optimal Euclidean length, given their terminal destinations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the tortuosity analysis.

claim: Analysis across cell types revealed no significant differences in mean tortuosities (ANOVA; [F(3,12): 1.2, p=0.3509]; Tukey HSD).
source: Analysis across cell types revealed no significant differences in mean tortuosities (ANOVA; [F(3,12): 1.2, p=0.3509]; Tukey HSD).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: It is qualitatively evident that the MSTs are not exact representations of the actual LP neuronal structure.
source: It is qualitatively evident that the MSTs are not exact representations of the actual LP neuronal structure.
evidence: This is an observation from the MST analysis shown in Figure 11.

claim: No single balancing factor (bf) value collectively recapitulates neurite length, branch order, and tortuosity distributions for each neuron.
source: Yet, no single bf factor collectively recapitulates each of these distributions for each neuron.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the MST analysis shown in Figure 11.

claim: This discrepancy in best-fit bf values across morphological metrics can be observed in all 16 STG neurons and disallows a confident assignment of bf value within or across neuron types.
source: This discrepancy in best-fit bf values across morphological metrics can be observed in all 16 STG neurons (Figure 11B, Figure 11—figure supplements 1–4) and disallows a confident assignment of bf value within or across neuron types.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the MST analysis shown in Figure 11 and supplements.

claim: This wiring cost equation alone appears insufficient to comprehensively recapitulate structural features of STG neurons.
source: Taken together, this wiring cost equation alone appears insufficient to comprehensively recapitulate these structural features of STG neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the MST analysis.

claim: It is plausible that STG neurite trees may simply not adhere to the wiring optimization principles enforced by this wiring cost equation.
source: It is plausible that STG neurite trees may simply not adhere to the wiring optimization principles enforced by this wiring cost equation.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the MST analysis.

claim: It remains unclear how tightly tuned or variable macroscopic and fine structural features must be in order to generate reliable physiological output in many neuron types.
source: Many neuron types present recognizable geometries. Yet, it remains unclear how tightly tuned or variable their macroscopic and fine structural features must be in order to generate reliable physiological output.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: The expansive and complex neuronal structures of STG neurons do not adhere to prevailing hypotheses regarding wiring optimization principles thought to govern developmental growth.
source: In the present study, we carried out a detailed morphometric analysis of four STG neuron types. We found that their expansive and complex neuronal structures do not adhere to prevailing hypotheses regarding wiring optimization principles thought to govern developmental growth.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the morphometric and MST analyses.

claim: Studies in insect nervous systems showed that spatially distinct dendritic subtrees compute a weighted integration of sensory inputs.
source: Work in insect nervous systems showed that spatially distinct dendritic subtrees compute a weighted integration of sensory inputs (Miller and Jacobs, 1984; Cuntz et al., 2008).
evidence: This references findings from previous studies.

claim: Studies in the mammalian retina and visual cortex have demonstrated that neurons receiving sensory inputs at distinct dendritic subtrees detect various visual stimulus features.
